Shuttle Puzzle Practice

PermutationsParity
Game: Draw bridges between the poles so that each top number slides down to the pole where the same number is written at the bottom.
How to play: Drag from one pole to another to draw a bridge. Press Verify when you think it works.
Look for the math

Walking down a pole and crossing every shuttle you meet takes each top to some bottom, and no two tops ever meet at the same bottom. So a set of shuttles is a permutation of the poles, and the puzzle asks you to build a given one.

One shuttle is one swap

Look at a single height. Above it, some top is travelling down each pole. A shuttle at that height between poles i and j swaps the two travellers on i and j and leaves the rest alone: it is a transposition (i,j). The shuttles read from the top down are a product of transpositions, which is what Show hint writes out.

Every target can be reached

Put the right traveller on pole 1 with one shuttle (or none, if it is there already), then the right one on pole 2, and so on. Each pole costs at most one shuttle, so every permutation is a product of transpositions. The logic test built such shuttles for every target with up to 6 poles (872 of them) and Verify accepted each one.

How few shuttles?

Write the target in cycles, as Show hint does: (1,3,2)(4)(5) has 3 cycles. A cycle of length k needs k − 1 swaps, so the fewest shuttles is N − (number of cycles), here 5 − 3 = 2. A breadth-first search over all lists of swaps confirmed that no shorter list exists for any target with up to 5 poles. You may use more, but every list for the same target has the same parity: extra shuttles always come in pairs.

Turn on Show hint, read the target's cycles, and try to solve it with exactly N minus the number of cycles shuttles.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
